title: Kyeema crash
place: Mount Dandenong, Victoria, Australia
summary: The airliner Kyeema was flying from Adelaide to Melbourne when it ran into thick fog. The crew thought they were further from Melbourne than they really were, so they flew past Essendon Airport. In the fog the aircraft struck Mount Dandenong close to the summit and nobody on board survived.
cause: The inquiry found the crew had mistaken one town for another through a gap in the cloud, which put their navigation about 30 km out. They then descended in fog without being able to see the ground.
lesson: Afterwards Australia introduced radio range navigation beacons that gave pilots an accurate course to follow in bad weather, and flight checking officers began monitoring aircraft. The inquiry also criticised delays in installing these beacons to save money.

title: Essendon King Air crash
place: Essendon Fields, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia
summary: A small charter aircraft was taking off from Essendon Airport for a flight to King Island. Seconds after leaving the runway it turned to the left and came down on the DFO shopping centre next to the airport. The pilot and four passengers died, and a few people on the ground were hurt.
cause: The Australian Transport Safety Bureau found the rudder trim had very likely been left in the wrong position before take-off. This made the aircraft yaw to one side and the pilot was not able to keep control so close to the ground.
lesson: The investigation highlighted how important it is for pilots to check every trim setting before take-off, and it encouraged better checklists and pre-flight checks for this type of aircraft.
wikipedia: 2017 Essendon Airport Beechcraft King Air crash

title: Mangalore mid-air collision
place: About 8 km south of Mangalore Airport, Victoria, Australia
aircraft: Piper PA-44-180 Seminole and Beechcraft D95A Travel Air
operator: Moorabbin Aviation Services (Seminole) and a private training flight from Tyabb (Travel Air)
summary: Two small twin-engine training aircraft collided in the air near Mangalore Airport in central Victoria. One was arriving to practise an instrument approach and the other was climbing away towards Essendon. Both aircraft were carrying two pilots, and all four died.
cause: The Australian Transport Safety Bureau found both crews had been told about the other aircraft but did not arrange to keep apart in airspace without air traffic control. The collision probably happened in or near cloud, so the pilots could not see each other.
lesson: The ATSB strongly encouraged pilots to fit and use ADS-B equipment, which shows nearby aircraft on a screen in the cockpit, and some versions are now available at low cost in Australia.

title: Frederick Valentich disappearance
place: Bass Strait, between Cape Otway and King Island, Australia
summary: Frederick Valentich, a 20 year old pilot, took off from Moorabbin Airport in Melbourne for a flight to King Island. Over Bass Strait he radioed Melbourne that he could see another aircraft with bright lights near him that he could not identify, and soon after the radio contact ended. He and his aircraft were never found, although part of an engine cowl that may have come from a Cessna 182 washed up on Flinders Island five years later.
cause: The Department of Transport investigation presumed the flight was fatal but could not determine the cause. Many theories have been suggested, but none has been proven.
lesson: Because the cause was never found, investigators made no specific changes. Today aircraft crossing open water usually carry emergency locator beacons, which help search teams find a missing aircraft much more quickly.

title: Emirates Flight 407 tailstrike
place: Melbourne Airport, Victoria, Australia
summary: A large Emirates airliner bound for Dubai was slow to speed up as it took off from Melbourne Airport at night. Its tail scraped along the runway and it only just lifted off past the end, clipping some lights and an antenna. The crew climbed away safely and returned to land at Melbourne with no one hurt.
cause: The first officer had typed in a take-off weight 100 tonnes lower than the real weight. The computers then worked out take-off speeds and engine power that were too low for the heavy aircraft.
lesson: Emirates made two pilots enter and cross-check the take-off data separately. Airbus improved its software to spot unlikely numbers, and work began on systems that warn pilots if the aircraft is not speeding up as it should.

title: Stinson Tokana crash
place: Near Redesdale and Mia Mia, Victoria, Australia
summary: The three-engine airliner Tokana left Essendon Airport for Broken Hill, with stops planned at Kerang and Mildura. About 21 minutes into the flight, witnesses near Redesdale heard a loud crack and saw the outer part of the left wing come away. The aircraft fell and all ten people on board died.
cause: Investigators found a fatigue crack in a welded part of the main wing spar. The crack had grown slowly over many flights until the wing failed in gusty weather.
lesson: Australia began setting safe working lives for metal aircraft parts, so that important parts are retired after a set number of flying hours before fatigue cracks can become dangerous.

title: Miss Hobart disappearance
place: Bass Strait, near Rodondo Island south of Wilsons Promontory, Australia
summary: Miss Hobart was a four-engine biplane airliner flying across Bass Strait between Launceston and Melbourne. Its last radio contact came over Rodondo Island, south of Wilsons Promontory, and then it vanished. Only small amounts of wreckage and oil were found and the eleven people on board were never located.
cause: The exact cause was never found. Later checks found faulty fin bias mechanisms on this aircraft type, which may have made it harder to control.
lesson: After this loss and another DH.86 loss in Bass Strait in 1935, authorities required stronger wing and tail bracing on these aircraft. One passenger was the father of David Warren, who later invented the flight data recorder in Melbourne.

title: RAAF Boeing 707 training crash
place: Bass Strait off Woodside Beach, south of East Sale, Victoria, Australia
summary: An air force Boeing 707 was on a peacetime training flight practising how to fly with engines on one side at low power. As it slowed down the pilots found it hard to control with the rudder. The aircraft stalled and spun into Bass Strait off the Gippsland coast and all five crew died.
cause: The Board of Inquiry found the training exercise itself was too dangerous and was almost certain to cause a loss of control. Gaps in training documents and lost experience within the squadron also contributed.
lesson: The RAAF improved its training manuals and syllabus for the 707 and changed how engine failure practice is carried out.

title: Lamington Stinson crash
place: McPherson Range, Lamington National Park, Queensland, Australia
summary: A Stinson airliner flying from Brisbane to Sydney disappeared in stormy weather over the rainforest-covered McPherson Range. Nine days later, local bushman Bernard O'Reilly worked out where it might be and walked through the rugged forest until he found the wreck. Two passengers, Joseph Binstead and John Proud, were still alive and were carried out by rescuers.
cause: The coroner found that a strong downdraft in the stormy weather most likely forced the aircraft down into the mountains.
lesson: The inquiry called for better weather reporting, central control of aerodromes and improved radio communication with aircraft.

title: Canberra air disaster
place: Near Canberra Airport, Australian Capital Territory, Australia
summary: An air force Hudson was flying from Melbourne to Canberra carrying three federal government ministers and the head of the Army. As it came in to land at Canberra it lost height and crashed into a paddock. All ten people on board died, which was a great shock to the nation.
cause: The Court of Inquiry found the aircraft stalled at low height on its landing approach, but the exact reason it stalled could not be determined. It was an accident, not a combat loss.
lesson: No specific safety changes are recorded. The air base at Canberra was later named Fairbairn in memory of the Minister for Air, James Fairbairn, who died in the crash.

title: Amana crash
place: Near York, Western Australia, Australia
summary: The airliner Amana took off from Perth at night bound for Adelaide. Soon afterwards people on the ground heard its engines running roughly, and about 18 minutes after take-off it came down in bushland near York. Everyone on board died, making it Australia's worst air accident at the time.
cause: The inquiry found the engines had lost power but could not work out why. Water in the fuel was suspected but could not be proven.
lesson: Fuel tankers had to be checked for water after refuelling, fuel samples had to be drained into clear containers so water could be seen, and pilots of four-engine aircraft had to do their check flights in four-engine aircraft.
wikipedia: 1950 Australian National Airways Douglas DC-4 crash

title: TAA Flight 538
place: Sea off Mackay, Queensland, Australia
summary: A Fokker Friendship flying from Brisbane was trying to land at Mackay at night in fog and low cloud. After two missed approaches the crew tried a third time, then radio contact stopped. The aircraft had come down in the sea about 3 nautical miles from the airport and no one survived.
cause: The cause was never determined. Investigators considered faulty altitude instruments, misreading of the altimeter, or the pilots losing their sense of height over the calm, dark sea.
lesson: Australia became the first country in the world to require cockpit voice recorders in airliners, and flight data recorders were recommended for passenger aircraft of this size. The flight recorder had been invented in Melbourne by David Warren.

title: Ansett-ANA Flight 149
place: Near Winton, Queensland, Australia
summary: A Viscount flying from Mount Isa to Longreach had a fire start in one of its engines. The crew could not put it out and turned towards Winton to land. The fire weakened the left wing, which failed before they reached the airport, and all 24 people on board died.
cause: Nuts holding an oil part on a cabin pressure blower inside the engine had come loose. This started a fire that spread to the fuel tank and weakened the wing.
lesson: The blower was redesigned so the part could not come loose. Investigators also found similar fires overseas had not been reported to the manufacturer, which showed how important it is to share safety information.

title: MacRobertson Miller Flight 1750
place: Near Port Hedland, Western Australia, Australia
summary: A Viscount flying from Perth to Port Hedland was descending towards its destination on New Year's Eve. Its right wing suddenly broke away and the aircraft fell to the ground on a station south of Port Hedland. All 26 people on board died.
cause: A fatigue crack had grown in the main wing spar. It started at a bolt hole that had been damaged during earlier maintenance work, which removed the protection against cracking.
lesson: All Australian Viscount 700 aircraft were grounded for checks, and the number of flights that key wing parts could be used for before replacement was cut from 11,400 to 7,000.

title: Southern Cloud disappearance
place: Snowy Mountains near Jagumba, New South Wales, Australia
summary: Southern Cloud was a three-engine airliner of Kingsford Smith and Ulm's airline, flying from Sydney to Melbourne in very bad weather. It disappeared and a big search found nothing. The wreck was finally discovered 27 years later, in 1958, by a worker in the Snowy Mountains.
cause: Severe weather is thought to have caused the crash. The wreck was found well off course and facing the wrong way, suggesting the crew became lost in the storm.
lesson: No formal changes are recorded, and the airline closed later in 1931. Parts of the aircraft are now kept in museums at Cooma and Tumbarumba.

title: Hobart DC-3 crash
place: Frederick Henry Bay, near Hobart, Tasmania, Australia
summary: A DC-3 took off from Cambridge Aerodrome in Hobart at night for Melbourne. Less than two minutes later it descended steeply into the sea with both engines still working. All 25 people on board died, which made it Australia's worst civil air accident at that time.
cause: The inquiry thought the most likely cause was the autopilot being switched on by mistake while one of its instruments was locked, but it could not be certain. It also found the captain had a medical condition that he had not reported, which probably contributed.
lesson: The inquiry recommended making the autopilot control look different from other controls, checking instruments before take-off, limiting training on passenger flights, and having aviation medical examiners appointed by the Department of Civil Aviation.

title: Whyalla Airlines Flight 904
place: Spencer Gulf, near Whyalla, South Australia, Australia
summary: A small twin-engine commuter aircraft was flying from Adelaide to Whyalla in the evening. The pilot radioed that both engines had failed and that he might have to land on the water. The aircraft came down in Spencer Gulf about 15 nautical miles from Whyalla and no one survived.
cause: The ATSB and the coroner disagreed. The ATSB blamed the way the engines were operated, while the coroner found one engine had a manufacturing defect in its crankshaft.
lesson: Life jackets became compulsory on passenger flights over water, along with other emergency equipment. The engine maker recalled about 1,000 engines worldwide to replace faulty crankshafts.

title: Lockhart River air disaster
place: Near Lockhart River, Cape York, Queensland, Australia
summary: A Metroliner flying from Bamaga to Cairns was descending through cloud to stop at Lockhart River. It hit a ridge called South Pap about 11 km from the airport. All 15 people on board died, the worst Australian civil air accident in decades.
cause: Investigators found the aircraft descended too low and too fast during its approach in cloud. The coroner found pilot error was the main cause, with weaknesses in the operator's training and procedures also involved.
lesson: The safety regulator cancelled the operator's licence to fly, and a Senate inquiry led to stronger oversight of airlines by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority and faster safety reforms.

title: Coulson C-130 air tanker crash
place: Peak View, Snowy Monaro, New South Wales, Australia
summary: During the Black Summer bushfires, a large air tanker was dropping fire retardant to help protect communities in southern New South Wales. Just after a drop, at low height, the aircraft lost height and crashed. The three American crew members, who had come to help fight Australia's fires, died.
cause: The ATSB found the aircraft probably stalled after the drop because of low-level wind shear and a stronger tailwind, which reduced its ability to climb while it was low and slow.
lesson: Coulson added wind shear recovery training and risk checks before each mission. The NSW Rural Fire Service created a Large Air Tanker Coordinator role and reviewed its aviation rules, including when crews can say no to a dangerous task.

title: Norfolk Island air ambulance ditching
place: Sea off Norfolk Island, Australia
summary: An air ambulance jet carrying a patient from Samoa to Melbourne planned to refuel at Norfolk Island. Bad weather stopped it landing and it did not have enough fuel to go anywhere else, so the pilot landed it on the sea at night. All six people got out and floated for about 90 minutes until local fishermen rescued them after spotting the captain's torch.
cause: Bad weather and not enough spare fuel meant the aircraft could not land or divert. The final investigation found the pilot's planning was at fault, but also that the rules for this type of flight were too relaxed.
lesson: A Senate inquiry criticised the first investigation for blaming only the pilot. The investigation was reopened, and its final report in 2017 also pointed to relaxed rules and weather information that was not passed on to the crew.

title: Qantas Flight 72
place: Over the Indian Ocean near Learmonth, Western Australia, Australia
summary: A Qantas A330 flying from Singapore to Perth suddenly pitched nose down twice while cruising at 37,000 feet. Passengers who were not wearing seatbelts were thrown around the cabin and many were hurt. The pilots regained control, declared an emergency and landed safely at Learmonth.
cause: One of the aircraft's three air data computers started sending wrong information. A design limitation in the flight control software meant the aircraft acted on that bad data and pushed the nose down.
lesson: Airbus gave airlines new procedures and Europe's safety agency issued an urgent order to fix the problem. The event is also a strong reminder to keep your seatbelt fastened whenever you are seated.

title: Mount Erebus disaster
place: Mount Erebus, Ross Island, Antarctica
summary: Flight 901 was a sightseeing flight from Auckland over Antarctica. The crew descended below cloud believing they were over the flat ice of McMurdo Sound, but they were heading straight for Mount Erebus. In whiteout conditions the white slope blended into the sky and the aircraft struck the mountain, and all 257 people on board died.
cause: The first report blamed the crew for descending too low. A later Royal Commission led by Justice Mahon found the main cause was that the airline had changed the flight path in the computer without telling the crew, so the route led over the mountain.
lesson: Sightseeing flights to Antarctica were stopped for many years. The disaster showed how important it is that pilots are told about every change to navigation data, and how whiteout can fool even experienced pilots.

title: Kaimai Range DC-3 crash
place: Kaimai Range, near Tauranga, New Zealand
summary: A DC-3 flying from Auckland to Tauranga in very poor weather struck a rock face in the Kaimai Range. All 23 people on board died. It is one of the worst air accidents in New Zealand's history.
cause: Investigators found a downdraft carried the aircraft below the tops of the range, into severe turbulence it could not climb out of. The crew had flown at the minimum safe height that was officially set at the time.
lesson: The Kaimai Range was reclassified as mountainous terrain and the minimum safe height for flying over it was raised by 1,000 feet.
wikipedia: New Zealand National Airways Corporation Flight 441

title: Ansett New Zealand Flight 703
place: Tararua Range, near Palmerston North, New Zealand
summary: A Dash 8 from Auckland was approaching Palmerston North in poor visibility when one of its main wheels would not come down. While the crew worked on the problem, the aircraft descended too low and hit hills in the Tararua Range. Seventeen people survived, and passenger Reginald Dixon was awarded the New Zealand Cross for helping others escape.
cause: New Zealand's Transport Accident Investigation Commission found the captain did not keep to the correct approach height while distracted by the landing gear problem. The ground proximity warning also gave too little time to react.
lesson: New Zealand passed a law in 1999 that protects accident investigation evidence, so that people can speak openly to investigators and lessons can be learned.

title: Moncrieff and Hood disappearance
place: Tasman Sea, west of New Zealand
summary: New Zealanders John Moncrieff and George Hood took off from Richmond near Sydney in the aircraft Aotearoa, trying to make the first flight across the Tasman Sea. Radio signals were heard for about 12 hours, when they should have been within a few hundred kilometres of New Zealand, and then stopped. Large air, sea and land searches never found them.
cause: The cause is unknown. The aircraft had no instruments to measure how far the wind was pushing it off course, and its radio could not help with navigation.
lesson: Later that year Kingsford Smith and Ulm made the first successful Tasman crossing in the Southern Cross, carrying a navigator and radio operator to help find their way.

title: Loss of the Lady Southern Cross
place: Andaman Sea, near Aye Island, off the coast of Myanmar (Burma)
summary: Sir Charles Kingsford Smith, Australia's most famous pioneer aviator, was flying overnight from India to Singapore with co-pilot Tommy Pethybridge, trying to set a new England to Australia speed record. Their aircraft, the Lady Southern Cross, disappeared over the Andaman Sea. Eighteen months later fishermen found a wheel and undercarriage leg from the aircraft at Aye Island.
cause: The cause is unknown because the main wreck has never been found.
lesson: There was no formal investigation. Kingsford Smith's pioneering flights helped prove the long-distance air routes that airlines later flew safely with better navigation, radio and larger crews.

title: Bert Hinkler's last flight
place: Pratomagno mountains, near Arezzo, Tuscany, Italy
summary: Bert Hinkler from Bundaberg was a record-breaking pilot who had made the first solo flight from England to Australia in 1928. In January 1933 he left London alone in his Puss Moth Karohi on another record attempt. His aircraft came down in the Pratomagno mountains of Italy and was later found by local charcoal burners.
cause: The exact cause is uncertain. Bad weather over the mountains is thought to have played a part, and the Puss Moth type had several wing failures in turbulence at that time.
lesson: No formal findings were made on his crash. The series of Puss Moth accidents in the early 1930s led to changes to the type to make it safer in rough air.

title: Qantas Flight 1
place: Don Mueang International Airport, Bangkok, Thailand
summary: A Qantas 747 flying from Sydney to London was landing in Bangkok during a heavy rainstorm. It touched down a long way along the wet runway, could not stop in time and ran off the end, coming to rest with its nose on a road beyond the runway. Everyone got off safely, although some people had minor injuries.
cause: Investigators found the approach was too high and fast, the touchdown was late, and the pilots did not communicate clearly when the go-around was cancelled. Standing water made the aircraft aquaplane on the runway.
lesson: The investigation highlighted the dangers of landing on flooded runways and the need for clear communication between pilots. Qantas repaired the aircraft so that it kept its record of no jet airliner losses.

title: Qantas Flight 30
place: Landed at Manila, Philippines, after an emergency over the South China Sea
summary: A Qantas 747 flying from Hong Kong to Melbourne was cruising at 29,000 feet when an emergency oxygen bottle in the cargo hold burst. It blew a large hole in the side of the aircraft and the cabin lost pressure, so oxygen masks dropped down. The pilots descended quickly to safe air and landed safely in Manila with no one hurt.
cause: The ATSB found one of the oxygen cylinders burst, but could not find a defect that would explain why.
lesson: The ATSB asked airlines and maintenance companies to review how they check and handle oxygen cylinders on aircraft.

title: Qantas Flight 32
place: Over Batam Island, Indonesia, then landed at Singapore Changi Airport
summary: Four minutes after leaving Singapore for Sydney, one engine of the Qantas A380 failed and pieces of it damaged the wing and many of the aircraft's systems. The crew spent almost two hours checking the damage while circling. They then landed safely back at Changi and everyone got off unhurt.
cause: A small oil pipe inside the Rolls-Royce engine had been made with a wall that was too thin. It cracked from fatigue, leaked oil and caused a fire that broke a turbine disc.
lesson: Airlines around the world urgently inspected their Trent 900 engines, and faulty engines were repaired or replaced.

title: First powered aeroplane fatality
place: Fort Myer, Virginia, United States
summary: Orville Wright was demonstrating his aeroplane to the United States Army with Lieutenant Thomas Selfridge as his passenger. A propeller cracked and the aeroplane dived into the ground. Orville was badly hurt but recovered, and Selfridge became the first person to die in a powered aeroplane accident.
cause: A split propeller hit a bracing wire, which pulled the rudder out of position and the pilot lost control.
lesson: The accident showed how important head protection was, and early military pilots began wearing helmets. It also pushed the Wright brothers to strengthen their propellers.

title: Amelia Earhart disappearance
place: Pacific Ocean, near Howland Island
summary: Amelia Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan were trying to fly all the way around the world near the equator. On the hardest leg, from New Guinea to tiny Howland Island in the Pacific, they lost radio contact and were never found. A huge search by the United States Navy and Coast Guard found no trace.
cause: Nobody knows for sure. The most widely accepted idea is that they could not find the small island, ran low on fuel and came down in the ocean.
lesson: Her flight showed how hard long-distance navigation over the ocean was, and how much pilots depended on good radio communication. Better radio navigation aids and procedures later made ocean crossings far safer.

title: Comet over Elba
place: Mediterranean Sea, off the island of Elba, Italy
summary: The Comet was the world's first jet airliner. Soon after leaving Rome on a flight from Singapore to London, it broke up at high altitude and fell into the sea near Elba. Nobody on board survived.
cause: Engineers tested a Comet in a giant water tank and found that metal fatigue had caused cracks to grow from the corners of openings in the cabin roof, until the cabin suddenly split open.
lesson: Aeroplanes are now designed and tested to resist metal fatigue, and windows and openings have rounded corners. The Comet investigation became a model for how accidents are studied today.

title: Grand Canyon mid-air collision
place: Grand Canyon, Arizona, United States
aircraft: Lockheed L-1049 Super Constellation and Douglas DC-7
operator: Trans World Airlines and United Air Lines
summary: Two airliners that had left Los Angeles a few minutes apart collided in the sky over the Grand Canyon. Both aeroplanes crashed into the canyon and nobody survived.
cause: Outside the main airways the pilots had to see and avoid each other themselves, with no radar watching them. Clouds and the limited view from the cockpits meant they did not see each other in time.
lesson: This accident led to the Federal Aviation Act of 1958, which created the agency now called the Federal Aviation Administration. Radar air traffic control was expanded across the United States so controllers could keep aeroplanes apart.

title: Munich air disaster
place: Munich-Riem Airport, Munich, West Germany
summary: The aeroplane was carrying the Manchester United football team home from a European Cup match. After two take-off attempts were abandoned, the third attempt failed and the aeroplane ran off the end of a snowy runway. Twenty-three people died, including eight players, and twenty-one survived.
cause: Slush on the runway slowed the aeroplane so much that it could not reach flying speed. The captain was at first blamed for ice on the wings, but a later inquiry cleared him.
lesson: The accident showed how dangerous slush and standing water on runways are. Rules were brought in for measuring runway conditions and for how much slush is allowed before an aeroplane can take off.

title: The Day the Music Died
place: Grant Township, near Clear Lake, Iowa, United States
summary: Rock and roll stars Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and The Big Bopper chartered a small aeroplane to their next concert after a show in Clear Lake, Iowa. It crashed into a farm field a few minutes after take-off on a snowy night. The pilot and all three musicians died.
cause: Investigators found the young pilot was not qualified to fly using instruments alone and flew into poor weather at night. He may also have misread an unfamiliar type of attitude instrument.
lesson: The accident is often used to show why pilots need instrument training before flying at night or in cloud. Weather briefings for pilots were also improved.

title: XB-70 mid-air collision
place: North of Barstow, California, United States
aircraft: North American XB-70 Valkyrie and Lockheed F-104 Starfighter
operator: United States Air Force and NASA
summary: The giant XB-70 Valkyrie was flying in close formation with four other aircraft for a publicity photo. A small F-104 jet drifted into its wing and struck its tail. Both aircraft crashed, and XB-70 pilot Alvin White escaped in his ejection capsule and survived.
cause: The aircraft were flying very close together, and the swirling air around the XB-70's huge wingtip is thought to have pulled the F-104 into it.
lesson: The accident led to much stricter rules for formation flying and photo flights involving test aircraft.

title: X-15 Flight 3-65-97
place: Near Randsburg, California, United States
operator: NASA and United States Air Force
summary: The X-15 rocket plane flew to the edge of space, more than 80 kilometres high. On the way down it went into a spin at very high speed and broke apart. Pilot Michael Adams died, the only death in the X-15 program.
cause: An electrical problem distracted the pilot, and he likely became confused about which way the aircraft was pointing. The control system then could not stop the spin.
lesson: Later research aircraft and spacecraft were given clearer displays showing the pilot which way the craft is heading, and better automatic control systems.

title: Miracle of the Andes
place: Andes mountains, Mendoza Province, Argentina, near the Chilean border
summary: The aeroplane was carrying a rugby team and their friends and family from Uruguay to Chile when it struck a mountain in the high Andes. The survivors sheltered in the snow for 72 days. Two of them, Nando Parrado and Roberto Canessa, walked for ten days across the mountains to find help, and sixteen people were rescued.
cause: The crew thought they had already crossed the mountains and began descending too early while flying in cloud.
lesson: The rescue showed the importance of being able to find a crash site quickly. Modern aircraft carry automatic emergency beacons that send their location to search teams.

title: Eastern Air Lines Flight 401
place: Florida Everglades, near Miami, United States
summary: While approaching Miami at night, the whole flight crew became busy checking a landing gear warning light. Nobody noticed the autopilot had been bumped off and the aeroplane slowly descended into the Everglades swamp. Rescuers in airboats helped 75 survivors.
cause: The crew were all focused on a burnt-out light bulb and did not monitor the aircraft's height.
lesson: This accident helped create Crew Resource Management, training that teaches pilots to share tasks and make sure someone is always flying and watching the aeroplane.

title: Tu-144 Paris Air Show crash
place: Goussainville, near Paris, France
summary: The Soviet supersonic Tu-144 was flying a display at the Paris Air Show. After a steep climb it dived, broke apart in the air and crashed into the village of Goussainville. The six crew and eight people on the ground died.
cause: The official cause was never clearly found. One idea is that the pilots made a sudden manoeuvre to avoid a French photography aircraft.
lesson: Air shows brought in stricter rules about where display aircraft can fly and how far they must stay from crowds and towns.
wikipedia: 1973 Paris Air Show Tupolev Tu-144 crash

title: Turkish Airlines Flight 981
place: Ermenonville Forest, near Paris, France
summary: Shortly after take-off from Paris, a rear cargo door burst open. The sudden loss of air pressure collapsed part of the cabin floor and damaged the control cables. The aeroplane crashed in a forest and nobody survived.
cause: The cargo door latch design made it possible for the door to seem locked when it was not. A similar problem had happened two years earlier on another DC-10.
lesson: DC-10 cargo doors were redesigned, and aircraft floors were strengthened or given vents so a sudden loss of pressure cannot damage the controls.

title: Tenerife airport disaster
place: Los Rodeos Airport, Tenerife, Canary Islands, Spain
summary: Many flights were diverted to the small Los Rodeos airport after an incident at another airport. In thick fog, a KLM 747 began its take-off while a Pan Am 747 was still on the same runway. It is the deadliest accident in aviation history, and 61 people on the Pan Am aeroplane survived.
cause: The KLM captain started the take-off without clearance. Radio calls were blocked and some words were misunderstood in the fog.
lesson: Air traffic control now uses strict standard phrases, and the word take-off is only used when giving clearance. Crew Resource Management training encourages every crew member to speak up if something seems wrong.

title: American Airlines Flight 191
place: Des Plaines, near O'Hare Airport, Chicago, United States
summary: As the DC-10 took off from Chicago, its left engine broke away from the wing. The aeroplane rolled over and crashed in a field near the airport, and nobody on board survived.
cause: Mechanics had used a forklift shortcut to remove and refit the engine, which cracked its mounting. When the engine fell off it also cut hydraulic lines that held the wing slats out.
lesson: Maintenance had to follow the manufacturer's approved methods exactly. Aircraft systems were changed so that slats stay in position even if hydraulics are lost.

title: Air Florida Flight 90
place: 14th Street Bridge, Potomac River, Washington, D.C., United States
summary: On a snowy afternoon, a Boeing 737 struggled to climb after take-off, hit a bridge and fell into the icy Potomac River. Five people on board survived. Bystanders and a park police helicopter crew helped pull them from the water.
cause: The crew did not turn on the engine anti-ice, so a sensor gave false readings and the engines produced less power than shown. Snow and ice on the wings also reduced lift.
lesson: Rules for de-icing aeroplanes and for how long they can wait before take-off in snow became much stricter. Pilot training on icing was improved.

title: British Airways Flight 9
place: Over Mount Galunggung, West Java, Indonesia
summary: At night over Indonesia, the 747 flew into an invisible cloud of volcanic ash from Mount Galunggung and all four engines stopped. The aeroplane glided for about 13 minutes while the crew kept trying to restart the engines. The engines came back to life and everyone landed safely in Jakarta.
cause: Volcanic ash melted inside the hot engines and clogged them. The ash could not be seen on the weather radar at night.
lesson: Volcanic Ash Advisory Centres were set up around the world to track ash clouds and warn pilots so aeroplanes can fly around them.

title: Air Canada Flight 797
place: Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport, Kentucky, United States
summary: A fire started in the rear toilet during the flight and smoke filled the cabin. The pilots made an emergency landing at Cincinnati, and 23 people escaped, but 23 others could not get out in time.
cause: The fire started in or near the rear toilet. The exact source was never confirmed, and it spread out of sight behind the walls.
lesson: Smoke detectors and automatic fire extinguishers were required in aeroplane toilets. Lights along the floor to guide people to the exits and fire-resistant seat covers were added to airliners.

title: Gimli Glider
place: Gimli, Manitoba, Canada
summary: Halfway through a flight from Montreal to Edmonton, a new Boeing 767 ran out of fuel and both engines stopped. Captain Bob Pearson, an experienced glider pilot, glided the aeroplane to a former air force base at Gimli. Everyone survived.
cause: Canada was changing to the metric system, and the fuel was worked out in pounds instead of kilograms, so the aeroplane had less than half the fuel it needed. A faulty fuel gauge also meant the crew could not check.
lesson: Airlines tightened their fuel calculation and checking procedures, and the mix-up showed how important it is to use the same units everywhere.

title: Japan Air Lines Flight 123
place: Mount Takamagahara, Ueno, Gunma Prefecture, Japan
summary: Twelve minutes after leaving Tokyo, the rear pressure wall of the 747 failed and damaged the tail and all the hydraulic systems. The pilots struggled for 32 minutes to control the aeroplane using only engine power before it struck a mountain. Four passengers were rescued the next day. It is the deadliest single-aircraft accident in history.
cause: A repair to the rear pressure bulkhead after an earlier tail strike had been done incorrectly, which let metal fatigue cracks grow.
lesson: Repair inspections became stricter, and aircraft were designed so a failure in the pressure wall cannot drain every hydraulic system. Japan Airlines opened a Safety Promotion Center to teach its staff about the accident.

title: Aloha Airlines Flight 243
place: In flight near Maui, Hawaii, United States
summary: On a short island hop in Hawaii, a large section of the cabin roof tore away at about 7,300 metres. The pilots landed safely at Kahului on Maui. Sadly one flight attendant was lost, but everyone else survived.
cause: The aeroplane had made a very large number of short flights in salty air. Corrosion and metal fatigue had weakened the joints in its skin and inspections did not find the damage.
lesson: The Federal Aviation Administration started an aging aircraft program with much more detailed inspections for older aeroplanes.

title: Kegworth air disaster
place: Near East Midlands Airport, Kegworth, England, United Kingdom
summary: One engine on a nearly new Boeing 737 failed while it was climbing. The pilots shut down the wrong engine and the aeroplane lost power just short of the runway, coming down beside a motorway. Seventy-nine people survived.
cause: The crew misread which engine had the fault. Cabin crew and passengers could see flames from the left engine, but this was not passed on to the pilots.
lesson: Engine instruments were made clearer and pilots were given more training on new aircraft types. Research from this accident improved the brace position and seat strength, and cabin crew are encouraged to tell pilots what they see.

title: United Airlines Flight 232
place: Sioux Gateway Airport, Sioux City, Iowa, United States
summary: The tail engine of the DC-10 broke apart and its pieces cut through all three hydraulic systems, so the normal controls stopped working. The crew, helped by a training pilot travelling as a passenger, steered by changing the power of the two wing engines. The aeroplane crash landed at Sioux City and 184 people survived thanks to their teamwork and a well-prepared rescue team.
cause: A hidden flaw made at the factory in a fan disc inside the engine had grown into a crack that was missed during inspection.
lesson: Engine parts are now inspected with better methods, and aircraft were changed so damage cannot drain all hydraulic systems. The crew's teamwork is still used to teach Crew Resource Management.

title: British Airways Flight 5390
place: Over Didcot, Oxfordshire, England, United Kingdom
summary: As the aeroplane climbed out of Birmingham, a cockpit windscreen blew out and Captain Tim Lancaster was pulled partly out of the window. Cabin crew held onto him while the co-pilot landed safely at Southampton. The captain recovered and everyone survived.
cause: The windscreen had been fitted the day before using bolts that were very slightly too small.
lesson: Maintenance rules were tightened so engineers must check they are using exactly the right parts and have safety-critical work double-checked.

title: Scandinavian Airlines Flight 751
place: Gottröra, near Stockholm, Sweden
summary: Clear ice broke off the wings during take-off from Stockholm and was sucked into both rear engines, which then failed. The pilots glided the aeroplane into a snowy field, where it broke into three pieces. Everyone survived.
cause: The ice on top of the wings had not been found or removed before take-off. An automatic system the pilots had not been told about also pushed the damaged engines to more power.
lesson: De-icing checks became more thorough, including touching the wing surfaces to feel for clear ice. Airlines also made sure pilots were trained on all automatic systems.

title: TWA Flight 800
place: Atlantic Ocean, near East Moriches, New York, United States
summary: Twelve minutes after leaving New York for Paris, the 747 broke apart over the Atlantic Ocean. Nobody survived. Investigators recovered most of the aeroplane from the sea and rebuilt it in a hangar to study it.
cause: Fuel vapour in the nearly empty centre fuel tank exploded, most likely set off by a spark from damaged wiring.
lesson: New rules require airliners to reduce the chance of fuel tank explosions, for example by filling tanks with nitrogen-rich air that will not burn. Wiring inspections were improved.

title: Swissair Flight 111
place: Atlantic Ocean, off Peggys Cove, Nova Scotia, Canada
summary: Soon after leaving New York for Geneva, the crew smelled smoke in the cockpit and began diverting to Halifax. A fire spread above the ceiling and the aeroplane crashed into the ocean near Peggys Cove. Nobody survived.
cause: Wiring for the in-flight entertainment system probably caused a spark, and insulation material behind the walls caught fire and spread it.
lesson: Flammable insulation was replaced across many airliners, and fire tests for aircraft materials became much stricter. Crews were also trained to land as soon as possible when there is smoke.

title: Concorde crash at Paris
place: Gonesse, near Paris, France
summary: During take-off from Paris, Concorde ran over a small metal strip that had fallen from another aircraft. A tyre burst and pieces hit a fuel tank, starting a fire. The aeroplane crashed into a hotel at Gonesse and nobody on board survived.
cause: The metal strip had fallen off a DC-10 that took off a few minutes earlier. The burst tyre caused a shock wave that ruptured the fuel tank.
lesson: Concorde was given Kevlar linings in its fuel tanks and stronger tyres before flying again. Airports also improved runway checks for debris.

title: Air Transat Flight 236
place: Lajes Air Base, Terceira Island, Azores, Portugal
summary: Over the Atlantic Ocean, the Airbus A330 ran out of fuel and both engines stopped. The pilots glided for about 19 minutes and more than 100 kilometres to an air base in the Azores. It is the longest glide by a passenger jet and everyone survived.
cause: A wrong part fitted to the right engine rubbed against a fuel line until it cracked. The crew did not realise there was a leak and moved fuel towards it.
lesson: Airbus added warnings and checklists to help pilots spot fuel leaks. Maintenance rules for using the correct parts were tightened.

title: Air France Flight 358
place: Toronto Pearson International Airport, Ontario, Canada
summary: The Airbus A340 landed in a heavy thunderstorm, ran off the end of the runway and slid into a ravine, where it caught fire. The cabin crew got all the passengers out in about two minutes, and everyone survived.
cause: The aeroplane landed too far along a wet runway with a tailwind, and the crew could not stop in time.
lesson: Canada was urged to add longer safety areas at the ends of runways. Pilots received better guidance on landing in storms, and the fast evacuation showed why passengers should listen to the safety briefing.

title: British Airways Flight 38
place: Heathrow Airport, London, England, United Kingdom
summary: As the Boeing 777 approached Heathrow after a flight from Beijing, both engines lost power. The crew stretched the glide over houses and roads and landed on the grass just short of the runway. Everyone survived.
cause: Ice crystals that had formed in the very cold fuel built up in a part of the fuel system called the fuel-oil heat exchanger and blocked the fuel flow.
lesson: Rolls-Royce redesigned the fuel-oil heat exchanger on its Trent 800 engines so ice could not block it.

title: Miracle on the Hudson
place: Hudson River, New York City, United States
summary: Minutes after take-off from LaGuardia Airport, the Airbus A320 flew into a flock of Canada geese and both engines lost power. Captain Chesley Sullenberger and First Officer Jeffrey Skiles landed on the Hudson River. Ferries and rescue boats picked everyone up and all 155 people survived.
cause: Bird strikes damaged both engines so badly that they could not produce enough power.
lesson: Engine bird strike tests and wildlife management near airports were reviewed. Training for water landings and for losing both engines at low height was improved.

title: Colgan Air Flight 3407
place: Clarence Center, near Buffalo, New York, United States
summary: On a winter night approach to Buffalo, the Q400 slowed down too much and its stall warning activated. The aeroplane crashed into a house, and nobody on board survived.
cause: The captain reacted to the stall warning in the wrong way. Tiredness and gaps in the crew's training also played a part.
lesson: The United States brought in tougher rules for airline pilots, including more flying experience before joining an airline, better stall training and new rest rules to fight tiredness.

title: Air France Flight 447
place: South Atlantic Ocean, between Brazil and Senegal
summary: Flying overnight from Rio de Janeiro to Paris, the Airbus A330 disappeared over the Atlantic Ocean. Some wreckage was found within days, but the flight recorders were not found on the deep sea floor until almost two years later. Nobody survived.
cause: Ice crystals blocked the speed sensors, the autopilot switched off and the pilots did not recognise that the aeroplane had stalled.
lesson: Speed sensors were replaced with better models, and pilots worldwide now practise recovering from stalls and unusual situations at high altitude. New ways of finding flight recorders in deep water were also developed.

title: Asiana Airlines Flight 214
place: San Francisco International Airport, California, United States
summary: Landing at San Francisco on a clear day, the Boeing 777 came in too low and slow and its tail hit the sea wall before the runway. The aeroplane slid along the ground and caught fire. Most people got out quickly, and 304 of the 307 people on board survived.
cause: The pilots did not manage the approach well and misunderstood how the automatic power system would behave, so the aeroplane slowed down too much.
lesson: Airlines put more focus on hand flying skills and on understanding automatic systems. The high survival rate also showed the value of strong seats and well trained cabin crew.

title: Malaysia Airlines Flight 370
place: Southern Indian Ocean, approximate search area west of Australia
summary: The Boeing 777 disappeared from radar on a night flight from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing. Satellite signals showed it kept flying for hours, probably ending far out in the southern Indian Ocean. Australia led an underwater search covering about 120,000 square kilometres, and some pieces of the aeroplane later washed up on islands and coasts near Africa.
cause: Unknown. The main wreckage has not been found, so investigators could not work out why the aeroplane turned off course.
lesson: Airliners are now required to report their position more often over remote oceans, and newer aircraft must be able to send out their location when in distress. Flight recorder location beacons now last longer.

title: SpaceShipTwo VSS Enterprise
place: Mojave Desert, near Cantil, California, United States
summary: During a powered test flight, the SpaceShipTwo spaceplane broke apart high over the Mojave Desert. Co-pilot Michael Alsbury died. Pilot Peter Siebold was thrown clear, his parachute opened and he survived.
cause: The co-pilot unlocked the tail feather system too early, and air forces then pushed it open at the wrong time. The design did not protect against this single mistake.
lesson: Virgin Galactic added a lock that stops the feather system being unlocked too early. Investigators also asked for stronger safety reviews of commercial spaceflight designs.

title: Lion Air Flight 610
place: Java Sea, off Karawang, Indonesia
summary: Minutes after leaving Jakarta, the new Boeing 737 MAX kept pointing its nose down while the pilots fought to climb. The aeroplane crashed into the Java Sea and nobody survived.
cause: A faulty sensor fed wrong information to new flight software called MCAS, which repeatedly pushed the nose down. Pilots had not been told about the system.
lesson: After a second similar accident, the 737 MAX was grounded worldwide for about 20 months. The software was redesigned to use two sensors and pilot training was updated.

title: Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302
place: Near Bishoftu, Ethiopia
summary: Six minutes after taking off from Addis Ababa, a Boeing 737 MAX crashed in a field and nobody survived. It was the second 737 MAX accident in less than five months.
cause: As with Lion Air Flight 610, a faulty sensor caused the MCAS software to repeatedly push the nose down.
lesson: Countries around the world grounded the 737 MAX. It returned to service only after its software was fixed and pilots were retrained, and aircraft certification rules were tightened.

title: Haneda runway collision
place: Haneda Airport, Tokyo, Japan
aircraft: Airbus A350-900 and De Havilland Canada Dash 8
operator: Japan Airlines and Japan Coast Guard
summary: A Japan Airlines A350 landing at Haneda collided with a Coast Guard aircraft that was on the runway, preparing to carry supplies to earthquake survivors. The A350 caught fire, but the cabin crew got all 379 passengers and crew out safely. Five of the six Coast Guard crew died.
cause: Investigators found the Coast Guard crew believed they had permission to enter the runway when they did not, and the mistake was not picked up in time. The final report is still pending.
lesson: Japan added extra controllers and warning systems to watch runways. Airlines around the world pointed to the calm evacuation, where nobody took their bags, as an example to follow.

title: Alaska Airlines Flight 1282
place: In flight over Portland, Oregon, United States
summary: Shortly after take-off from Portland, a panel called a door plug blew out of the side of the cabin. The pilots returned safely to Portland. The two seats next to the panel were empty, and everyone survived with only minor injuries.
cause: Investigators found the four bolts that hold the door plug in place had not been put back after work at the Boeing factory.
lesson: Similar aircraft were grounded for inspections, and the Federal Aviation Administration greatly increased its checks of Boeing's factory work.

title: Jeju Air Flight 2216
place: Muan International Airport, South Korea
summary: Returning from Bangkok, the Boeing 737 hit a flock of birds as it approached Muan. The crew made a second approach and landed without the wheels down, sliding off the runway into a solid mound that held landing equipment. Two cabin crew at the back were rescued.
cause: The final report is still pending. Investigators are looking at the bird strike, which engine was shut down, why the wheels were not lowered and the solid mound at the end of the runway.
lesson: South Korea began rebuilding solid structures near the ends of runways at several airports so they would break away if hit. Bird control at airports is also being reviewed.

title: Potomac River mid-air collision
place: Potomac River, Washington, D.C., United States
aircraft: Bombardier CRJ700 and Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk
operator: PSA Airlines for American Eagle, and United States Army
summary: An airliner coming in to land at Reagan National Airport at night collided with an Army helicopter on a training flight over the Potomac River. Both aircraft fell into the river and nobody survived.
cause: The NTSB final report in 2026 found the main cause was a helicopter route placed too close to the runway approach path, along with weak oversight and too much reliance on pilots seeing each other.
lesson: Helicopter routes near the airport were closed or changed, and flights near busy airports now rely more on controllers and electronic systems that show where other aircraft are.

title: Delta Connection Flight 4819
place: Toronto Pearson International Airport, Ontario, Canada
summary: In gusty winter winds, the CRJ900 landed hard at Toronto, lost a wing and flipped upside down on the snowy runway. Passengers hung in their seatbelts and then climbed out, and rescue crews arrived within moments. Everyone survived.
cause: The final report is still pending. Early findings show a hard landing broke part of the landing gear.
lesson: The accident showed how strong modern seats, seatbelts and fast airport rescue teams help people survive. Further lessons will come from the final report.

title: Air India Flight 171
place: Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India
summary: Seconds after taking off from Ahmedabad for London, the Boeing 787 lost power and came down on buildings of a medical college. One passenger survived. It was the first fatal accident involving a 787.
cause: The final report is still pending. A preliminary report found the switches that send fuel to both engines moved to the off position just after take-off, but why this happened has not been officially explained.
lesson: Airlines in India and elsewhere checked the fuel control switches on their aircraft. More lessons are expected when the final report is published.

title: Pan Am Flight 103
place: Lockerbie, Scotland, United Kingdom
summary: A Boeing 747 flying from London to New York broke apart high above the small Scottish town of Lockerbie, about 38 minutes after take-off. Everyone on board was lost, and 11 people in the town also died. It remains the deadliest act of terrorism in the history of the United Kingdom.
cause: A bomb hidden inside a suitcase in the cargo hold. A Scottish court convicted a Libyan intelligence officer in 2001, and Libya later accepted responsibility.
lesson: Airports began checking that every bag in the hold belongs to a passenger who is actually on the plane, and screening of checked bags became much stricter. The victims are remembered at a memorial garden near Lockerbie and at Arlington National Cemetery in the United States.

title: American Airlines Flight 11
place: North Tower, World Trade Center, New York City, United States
summary: On the morning of 11 September 2001 a flight from Boston to Los Angeles was taken over by terrorists soon after take-off. They flew it into the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York, and the tower later collapsed. It was the first of four planes used in the attacks that day.
cause: A group of terrorists hijacked the plane as part of a planned attack on the United States. The figures on board include the five hijackers.
lesson: After 11 September, airliners were fitted with strong locked cockpit doors and airport security screening became much stricter around the world. The National September 11 Memorial in New York has two large reflecting pools where the towers once stood, with the names of everyone who died.

title: United Airlines Flight 175
place: South Tower, World Trade Center, New York City, United States
summary: A flight from Boston to Los Angeles was taken over by terrorists and flown into the South Tower of the World Trade Center, about 17 minutes after the first plane hit the North Tower. Firefighters, police and ordinary people worked bravely to help others escape before the towers fell.
cause: A group of terrorists hijacked the plane as part of the coordinated attacks of 11 September 2001. The figures on board include the five hijackers.
lesson: Cockpit doors were strengthened and locked, and screening of passengers and bags became far more thorough. The names of all the victims are written around the memorial pools in New York.

title: American Airlines Flight 77
place: The Pentagon, Arlington County, Virginia, United States
summary: A flight from Washington Dulles to Los Angeles was taken over by terrorists and flown into the Pentagon, the headquarters of the United States military. Everyone on board and 125 people in the building were lost.
cause: A group of terrorists hijacked the plane as part of the coordinated attacks of 11 September 2001. The figures on board include the five hijackers.
lesson: Airline security changed around the world, with locked cockpit doors and stricter screening. The Pentagon Memorial has 184 benches, one for each person who died on the plane and in the building.

title: United Airlines Flight 93
place: Near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, United States
summary: This flight from Newark to San Francisco was the fourth plane taken over by terrorists on 11 September 2001. After hearing by phone about the other attacks, the passengers and crew bravely fought back to retake the plane. It came down in a field near Shanksville, far from its intended target, which is believed to have been in Washington.
cause: A group of terrorists hijacked the plane as part of the coordinated attacks. The courage of the passengers and crew stopped it from reaching its target. The figures on board include the four hijackers.
lesson: The Flight 93 National Memorial now stands in the field, including the Tower of Voices with 40 wind chimes, one for each passenger and crew member. Locked cockpit doors and stronger screening were introduced on airliners everywhere.

title: Malaysia Airlines Flight 17
place: Near Hrabove, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine
summary: A Boeing 777 flying from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur was destroyed over eastern Ukraine, where a war was being fought on the ground. All 298 people on board were lost, including 38 people who called Australia home, many of them from Victoria.
cause: A missile fired from the ground during the war in eastern Ukraine. An international investigation found the missile system had been brought from Russia, and a Dutch court convicted three men in 2022. Russia denies any responsibility.
lesson: Airlines and governments now share much better information about dangerous airspace over conflict zones, and planes are routed away from it. The Australian victims are remembered with a memorial at Parliament House in Canberra.

title: Korean Air Lines Flight 007
place: Sea of Japan, near Moneron Island, west of Sakhalin, Russia
summary: A Boeing 747 flying from New York to Seoul, via Anchorage, drifted far off course and into Soviet airspace during the Cold War. It was shot down by a Soviet fighter jet and came down in the sea near Moneron Island.
cause: A navigation mistake took the airliner into closed military airspace, where Soviet forces treated it as a threat and fired on it.
lesson: Soon afterwards the United States announced that its GPS satellite navigation system would be made available for civilian use, which helps aircraft and people everywhere know exactly where they are today.

title: Iran Air Flight 655
place: Strait of Hormuz, near Qeshm Island, Iran
summary: A short passenger flight from Bandar Abbas in Iran to Dubai was shot down over the Strait of Hormuz, at a time when warships were in the area during the Iran and Iraq war. All 290 people on board were lost.
cause: A missile fired by the American warship USS Vincennes. The United States said the crew mistook the airliner for a military jet, while Iran said the attack was reckless. The reasons are still disputed.
lesson: In 1996 the United States agreed to pay compensation to the families. The event is still remembered each year in Iran, and it is studied as a lesson in how military forces must identify civilian aircraft carefully.

title: Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752
place: Shahriar County, near Tehran, Iran
summary: A Boeing 737 flying from Tehran to Kyiv was shot down a few minutes after take-off, during a time of high military tension. All 176 people on board were lost, many of them students and families from Canada and Iran.
cause: Two missiles fired by Iran's Revolutionary Guard, whose air defence crew mistook the airliner for a hostile target. Iran admitted this three days later and called it human error.
lesson: It reminded the world that countries must close their skies to passenger flights when their military forces are on high alert. Families of the victims continue to campaign for answers and remembrance.

title: Air India Flight 182
place: Atlantic Ocean, about 190 km off County Cork, Ireland
summary: A Boeing 747 flying from Montreal to London, on its way to India, broke apart over the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Ireland. All 329 people on board were lost, most of them Canadians. People from the nearby Irish coast helped with the search.
cause: A bomb hidden in a suitcase in the cargo hold, placed by a group of terrorists. A related bomb exploded the same day at Narita Airport in Japan.
lesson: Security checks on luggage became much stricter, including making sure that no bag flies without its owner. Memorials stand at Ahakista in Ireland and in Toronto, and Canada holds a national day of remembrance for victims of terrorism on 23 June.

title: Germanwings Flight 9525
place: Prads-Haute-Bléone, French Alps, France
summary: An Airbus A320 flying from Barcelona to Düsseldorf came down in the French Alps during its flight. All 150 people on board were lost, including a group of school students and their teachers.
cause: The co-pilot, who was unwell, locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately flew the plane into the mountains, according to the French investigation.
lesson: For a time many airlines required two crew members to be in the cockpit at all times. Airlines and regulators also put much more focus on pilots' mental health, with support programs where pilots can safely ask for help.

title: Ethiopian Airlines Flight 961
place: Indian Ocean, near Le Galawa Beach, Grande Comore, Comoros
summary: Three hijackers took over a flight from Addis Ababa to Nairobi and demanded to be flown much further than the fuel allowed. When the fuel ran out, the captain skilfully steered the plane down into the shallow sea next to a beach in the Comoro Islands. Tourists, scuba divers and holidaying doctors rushed to help, and 50 people survived.
cause: A group of hijackers forced the crew to keep flying until the plane ran out of fuel. The figures include the three hijackers.
lesson: Many passengers who inflated their life jackets inside the cabin could not get out, which is why flight attendants remind everyone to inflate life jackets only after leaving the plane. The captain and the rescuers were praised for their courage.

title: Lufthansa Flight 181 rescue
place: Mogadishu International Airport, Somalia
summary: A Lufthansa flight from Mallorca to Frankfurt, an aircraft named Landshut, was hijacked and flown across many countries over five days. At Mogadishu in Somalia, a special German police team boarded the plane and freed all the hostages in about seven minutes. Sadly the captain, Jürgen Schumann, had been killed by the hijackers earlier.
cause: A group of terrorists hijacked the plane to demand the release of prisoners. Three of the four hijackers died in the rescue.
lesson: The rescue showed how well-trained rescue teams could free hostages safely, and many countries built similar teams. The Landshut was brought home to Germany in 2017 so the story can be remembered.

title: Air France Flight 8969 rescue
place: Marseille Provence Airport, France
summary: An Air France flight was hijacked at Algiers airport and later flown to Marseille in France. There, a French police rescue team called the GIGN stormed the plane and freed everyone still on board. Sadly three passengers had been killed before the plane left Algiers.
cause: A group of armed terrorists took over the plane. All four hijackers died in the rescue and are included in the figures.
lesson: The rescue is still studied by security teams around the world. It also warned governments that terrorists might try to use airliners as weapons.

title: Dawson's Field hijackings
place: Dawson's Field, near Zarqa, Jordan
aircraft: Boeing 707, Douglas DC-8 and Vickers VC10
summary: In September 1970 three passenger jets were hijacked and flown to a remote desert airstrip in Jordan called Dawson's Field. About 310 passengers and crew were held as hostages. The planes were blown up on 12 September once they were empty, and all of the hostages were eventually released.
cause: A group of terrorists hijacked the planes to demand the release of prisoners. Nobody on these three aircraft was killed.
lesson: Soon afterwards the United States started its sky marshal program, placing armed security officers on flights, and airports began screening passengers before boarding.

title: Operation Entebbe
place: Entebbe International Airport, Uganda
summary: An Air France flight from Tel Aviv to Paris was hijacked and flown to Entebbe in Uganda, where many passengers were held as hostages for a week. The Air France crew bravely refused to leave the remaining hostages. Israeli commandos flew thousands of kilometres overnight and rescued 102 of the 106 hostages, though sadly four hostages and one commando died.
cause: A group of terrorists hijacked the plane to demand the release of prisoners. Exact figures for everyone on board are complicated because some hostages were freed earlier.
lesson: The rescue became one of the most famous in history. The Air France captain and crew were honoured for staying with their passengers.

title: Azerbaijan Airlines Flight 8243
place: Near Aktau International Airport, Kazakhstan
summary: An Embraer jet flying from Baku to Grozny in Russia was damaged as it approached Grozny, then flew across the Caspian Sea and crashed near Aktau in Kazakhstan. The crew kept the damaged plane flying for a long time, and 29 people survived.
cause: The preliminary report found the plane was hit by fragments of a Russian air defence missile. Russia's president later admitted this, and in 2026 Russia and Azerbaijan agreed it was an unintentional strike. The final report is still to come.
lesson: It is another reminder that passenger flights must be kept well away from areas where air defences are active. The two pilots and a flight attendant, who lost their lives, were named National Heroes of Azerbaijan for their bravery.

title: Death of the Red Baron
place: Near Vaux-sur-Somme, France
summary: Manfred von Richthofen, the most famous fighter pilot of the First World War, was shot down while flying low over the Somme in his red Fokker triplane. He was known as the Red Baron and had won 80 air combat victories. His plane landed in a field near Vaux-sur-Somme, close to Australian troops.
cause: He was hit by a single bullet during a chase near the ground. The Royal Air Force credited Canadian pilot Roy Brown, but most historians now think an Australian machine gunner on the ground fired the shot. This is still debated.
lesson: Australian airmen of No. 3 Squadron gave him a full military funeral with honour, showing respect for a brave opponent. The Australian War Memorial in Canberra holds his control column and flying boots.

title: Lady Be Good
place: Libyan Desert, Libya
summary: This American bomber was flying home from a raid in the Second World War when it flew past its base in the dark and kept going far into the Sahara Desert. The crew parachuted out, thinking they were over the sea. The plane was not found until 1958, when oil explorers spotted it about 710 km inland.
cause: The young crew lost their way at night, and a faulty direction finder meant they did not know they had passed their base.
lesson: The crew's diary showed how bravely they kept walking north through the desert to find help. Parts of the plane are now displayed at the National Museum of the United States Air Force.

title: Glenn Miller's disappearance
place: Over the English Channel
summary: Glenn Miller, a famous American bandleader who played music for troops in the Second World War, took off from England in a small single-engine plane bound for Paris. The plane was never seen again, and no trace of it has ever been found.
cause: An official inquiry decided the plane most likely came down over the English Channel because of bad weather, a mechanical problem or pilot error. Other ideas have been suggested, so the cause is still a mystery.
lesson: His name is listed on the Wall of the Missing at the Cambridge American Cemetery in England, and his music is still played around the world.

title: Destruction of the An-225 Mriya
place: Hostomel Airport, near Kyiv, Ukraine
summary: The An-225 Mriya, the largest aircraft ever built, was destroyed in its hangar during fighting at Hostomel Airport in the first days of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Nobody was on board, as the plane was waiting for an engine change.
cause: It was caught on the ground when the airport became a battlefield. Ukraine says it was destroyed by Russian forces.
lesson: Mriya means dream in Ukrainian, and Antonov has said it hopes to finish a second An-225 using a part-built airframe. Only one was ever completed.

title: Bakers Creek air crash
place: Bakers Creek, near Mackay, Queensland, Australia
summary: A B-17 carrying American soldiers back to New Guinea after leave crashed in fog soon after taking off near Mackay. Only one person survived. It is the deadliest air crash ever in Australia.
cause: The cause was never found. Because of wartime secrecy, the crash was not reported in the news at the time.
lesson: A memorial was unveiled at Bakers Creek in 1992, and another at Arlington in the United States in 2009, so the men are now remembered in both countries.

title: Metrojet Flight 9268
place: Near Housna, North Sinai, Egypt
summary: An Airbus A321 carrying holidaymakers home from Sharm El Sheikh in Egypt to Saint Petersburg in Russia broke apart over the Sinai Peninsula. All 224 people on board were lost.
cause: A bomb hidden on board by a terrorist group, according to Russian investigators.
lesson: Many countries stopped flights to the area for a time, and airports tightened security checks on their own workers as well as on passengers.

title: 1960 U-2 incident
place: Near Sverdlovsk (now Yekaterinburg), Russia
summary: An American U-2 spy plane flying very high over the Soviet Union during the Cold War was brought down by a missile. The pilot, Francis Gary Powers, parachuted to safety but was captured.
cause: A missile fired by Soviet air defences while the plane was on a secret photography mission.
lesson: Powers was freed in 1962 in a famous prisoner swap on the Glienicke Bridge in Berlin. The incident pushed both sides to rely more on satellites to take pictures from space.

title: QantasLink Flight 1737
place: Over Victoria, shortly after departing Melbourne Airport, Australia
summary: About ten minutes after a QantasLink flight took off from Melbourne for Launceston, a passenger tried to force his way to the cockpit. Flight attendants bravely stopped him, and passengers helped hold him until the plane landed safely back at Melbourne. Two flight attendants were hurt, but everyone on board survived.
cause: A passenger attempted to hijack the plane. Quick action by the cabin crew and passengers stopped him from reaching the pilots.
lesson: Qantas reviewed its security and fitted secure cockpit doors on all its aircraft by November 2003. The crew were praised for their courage.

title: Hindenburg disaster
place: Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey, United States
summary: The Hindenburg, a giant German passenger airship, caught fire while landing at Lakehurst after crossing the Atlantic. It was destroyed in under a minute, yet 62 of the 97 people on board survived. Ground crew bravely ran towards the airship to help people escape.
cause: The investigation found that leaking hydrogen gas was most likely set alight by a spark of static electricity.
lesson: The disaster ended the age of passenger airships. Modern airships and blimps use helium, which cannot burn.

title: R101 airship
place: Near Allonne, Beauvais, France
summary: Britain's huge new airship R101 was on its first long flight, heading for Karachi in India by way of Egypt, when it came down on a hillside in northern France during bad weather. It caught fire, and only six of the 54 people on board survived.
cause: The inquiry found that a tear in the outer cover probably let a gas bag fail, making the airship too heavy at the front to stay up.
lesson: Britain stopped building large airships soon afterwards. The crew are buried together at Cardington, and a memorial stands near the crash site in France.

title: 2020 Calabasas helicopter crash
place: Calabasas, California, United States
summary: A helicopter flying basketball star Kobe Bryant, his daughter Gianna and seven others to a youth basketball game crashed into hills in thick fog near Los Angeles. Everyone on board was lost.
cause: The pilot kept flying into cloud, became disorientated and lost control, according to the US safety investigators.
lesson: Investigators called for better training for flying in poor weather and for more helicopters to carry warning systems that alert pilots when they are close to the ground.

title: Gold Coast helicopter collision
place: Gold Coast Seaway near Sea World, Queensland, Australia
summary: Two sightseeing helicopters collided in mid-air near Sea World on the Gold Coast, one taking off and one coming in to land. Four people on the departing helicopter were lost. The pilot of the other helicopter landed safely on a sandbank, and members of the public and emergency crews rushed to help.
cause: The Australian Transport Safety Bureau found that the radio in the departing helicopter was faulty, so the pilots did not hear each other's calls. The operator had also not acted on earlier near misses.
lesson: The investigation stressed how important working radios, good lookout and a strong safety culture are for busy helicopter operations.
